question: The EU considers carbon capture and storage (CCS) funndamental pillars for the competitiveness of hard-to-abate sectors and the goals of the Net-Zero Industry Act. However, the latest Connecting Europe Facility (CEF Energy) call for proposals excluded CCS projects from the EUR 650 million earmarked for that call, creating deep uncertainty for the industrial sector.

While the Innovation Fund provides financing for CO2 capture sites, the paucity of CEF support for transport and storage may undermine investment in CCS, which operators consider the only sustainable way to prevent deindustrialisation. Plans are afoot for a regulatory package for CO2 transport; however, the global market calls for clear political direction and meaningful action.
Can the Commission answer the following questions: 1.

Will it acknowledge that the absence of CEF financing for transport and storage is at odds with the value chain approach taken in the Net-Zero Industry Act, and how does it intend to remedy this state of affairs to prevent capital flight?

Apart from a possible increase to the CEF budget or future CO2 regulatory frameworks, what financial instruments will it use to ensure that carbon capture projects that have already received funding have the right infrastructure by 2030?

Does it agree that, with a view to establishing a roadmap that does away with piecemeal financing, CCS should be given priority in high-level political dialogue with Member States and industry leaders, and if so, within what time frame?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (9.7.2026) The Connecting Europe Facility for Energy (CEF-E) provides financing for projects of common interest and projects of mutual interest, including cross-border carbon dioxide transport and storage infrastructure1. The CEF-E award decisions follow a transparent and competitive process assessed by independent external experts and the Commission2.

Since 2014, CEF-E has provided financial support in grants amounting to EUR 973 million to Carbon Dioxide (CO2) projects. More than 20 CO2 storage projects are under development in the EU, including three projects that already received storage permits3. Seven additional CO2 storage projects are applying for a permit in the EU.

In total, these sites could contribute more than 19 million tonnes per year in CO2 injection capacity. Demand for storage still exceeds the foreseen supply, making it urgent that Member States make full use of the framework established by the Net-Zero Industry Act4 (NZIA) and recognise all projects as Net-Zero Strategic Projects.

Member States should also provide streamlined permit-granting and financial support from their emission trading system (ETS) revenues. Without prejudice to the outcome of the negotiations on the next multiannual financial framework, strategic CO2 infrastructure could also be supported through the national regional and partnership plans and the European Competitiveness Fund proposals.

The latter also foresees support to net-zero strategic projects and to scale-up net-zero value chains. The Commission is currently implementing and preparing a number of measures seeking to foster improvements to the investment and deployment of Industrial Carbon Management5 value chains. In that context it will engage with Member States and stakeholders.

1 Falling under the energy infrastructure categories set out in point (5) of Annex II of Regulation (EU) 2022/869. 2 In accordance with the CEF Regulation (EU) 2021/1153 which lays down the rules governing how EU

financial support is awarded and managed. 3 The Greensand site in Denmark, the Porthos site in the Netherlands, and the Prinos site in Greece. 4 Regulation (EU) 2024/1735. 5 COM/2024/62 final, Towards an ambitious Industrial Carbon Management for the EU.
